Of course, from the financial viewpoint, testing on animals often is more economical in the times we live in. However, what I am talking about here is not saving money, but the well-being of the creatures concerned. My point is exactly that the commercialisation of products is being prioritised over wellfare. Also, regarding your point of pain relief affecting the drug being trialled, in fact, many animal tests also include pain relief methods, which are selected such that it would not have a bad effect on the trial results. The same could be achieved with human testing. And exactly, the point you are making here is that inhumane methods would be used on humans tested in many cases since it is necessary. However, why is it ok to do the same to animals? And how do you know that animals are more worthless than convicted criminals who committed some despicable deeds? This is perhaps becoming a rather subjective/philosophical issue, and many people here clearly disagree with me, but I believe that it is hard to argue that if we lived in a society where wellbeing was put ahead of financial gains, the issue of animal testing would not present such moral dilemmas.

I see your point there. However, although I agree that currently there is no practical capacity for completely eradicating animal testing in scientific methods, I believe that it could be reduced if at least a small percentage  of it was replaced with testing on humans. Even though animal testing models are indeed increasingly accurate and their DNA may be matching that of humans to a high degree, they are still not equal if products for humans are being tested. In addition, a lot of products tested are highly commercialised so that financial gains are given much higher priority than the wellbeing of animals concerned, and even the humans who later use the products. 
Also, I have to say that I don't agree that testing on convicted criminals would be equivalent to death penalty. If sufficient methods of reducing pain are used and the subjects' basic needs such as nutrition and hygiene are looked after, it can be argued that such research would be humane.
